_note: Fictional sources for teaching: every source cited here is invented. See sources.json.
title: Lost in translation
context: A nursing student has paraphrased a study about loneliness. The wording is their own — but compare it with the original.
question: What is the main problem with this paraphrase?

sourcePassage.text: Older adults who joined a weekly walking group reported less loneliness after six months than those on a waiting list. The effect was found only among participants who attended at least half of the sessions.

text: Loneliness is a serious problem for many older people, and it is linked to poorer physical and mental health. Many older adults live alone, especially after the death of a partner. Joining a walking group cures loneliness in older adults, as people who take part feel much less lonely within a few weeks {{cite:byrne2019}}. Walking groups are also cheap to run and easy to organise in most communities. GP surgeries should therefore refer all lonely older patients to a local walking group, as this is a simple solution that would quickly solve the problem for most people who are affected by it.

problems.text: The paraphrase changes what the study found.
problems.feedback: Yes. 'Reported less loneliness' has become 'cures loneliness', 'after six months' has become 'within a few weeks', and the condition about attending half the sessions has disappeared. The words are the student's own, but the meaning is no longer the source's.

problems.text: It is patchwriting: too close to the original wording.
problems.feedback: Look again — the wording is quite different from the original. This paraphrase has the opposite problem: it has moved too far from what the source actually says.
It reports the study's main finding, from the abstract, so no page number is needed. The problem is what the sentence claims.

problems.text: It should name the author in the sentence.
problems.feedback: Naming the author is a choice, not a requirement. The bracketed citation is fine; the problem is the content of the sentence.

repaired: Loneliness is a serious problem for many older people, and it is linked to poorer physical and mental health. Many older adults live alone, especially after the death of a partner. [[c1:Walking groups may help: older adults who joined a weekly group reported feeling less lonely after six months than people still waiting for a place {{cite:byrne2019}}.]] [[c2:The benefit, however, appeared only among those who went to at least half of the sessions.]] [[c3:Referral alone may therefore not be enough. GP surgeries that refer lonely patients to walking groups might also need to find ways to help them keep attending.]]

annotations.c1: The finding is reported at its real strength ('reported feeling less lonely', 'after six months') and with its comparison group.
annotations.c2: The condition the student left out is restored. It turns out to be the most useful part of the finding for practice.
annotations.c3: The writer's recommendation now follows from what the study found, rather than from an exaggerated version of it.

notes.text: In health sciences, readers may act on what you report, so a paraphrase must keep a finding's strength, timescale and conditions. Changing 'reported less loneliness' to 'cures loneliness' is a factual error, not a style choice.

chefsNote: A remix changes the recipe card, never the taste of the dish.
